MARKET.head: Australian wine's small formats gain ground amid moderation and single-person households
MARKET.summ: Consumer demand for wine is changing globally, and while this has shown up in many mature markets as a decline in consumption, the shift in consumption habits has also uncovered an increasing consumer interest in smaller, more flexible packaging formats.
takeaways: Combined export and domestic off-trade sales of 187mL wine packs rose 22% to almost 1.9 million litres in 2025-26.
Export volumes of 187mL packs grew 39% from 450,000 litres in 2023-24 to 620,000 litres in 2025-26, concentrated in Asia-Pacific.
Single-person households make up 26% of Australian households, up from 18% in 1981, per Census data cited in the bulletin.

MARKET.head: EU greenwashing rules restrict vague eco claims on wine labels and marketing
MARKET.summ: New restrictions on environmental marketing claims are putting terms like “natural” and “eco-friendly” under the microscope, prompting questions about what wineries can and can’t include on bottle labels
takeaways: EU Directive 2024/825, enforced from September 27, bans vague environmental claims like "eco-friendly" and unverified sustainability badges on wine.
Old stock is not grandfathered in, so producers are using stickers or point-of-sale information to fix existing inventory.
Fines can reach four percent of annual turnover, with enforcement left to each member state's own framework.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux takes 41% of week's traded wine value as Burgundy's share jumps
MARKET.summ: Bordeaux strengthened its lead of the market, claiming 41% of traded value. Burgundy’s share also rose compared to last week
takeaways: Bordeaux claimed 41% of the week's traded value on Liv-ex, with 2019 and 2020 vintages top-traded.
Burgundy's share of traded value rose from 15.7% to 20.8%, with Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and Domaine Leflaive leading.
Champagne's share fell from 13.0% to 8.5%, while Tuscany claimed 11.6% led by Soldera Case Bassa and Sassicaia.

MARKET.head: California table grape supply to hold through December for holiday retail promotions
MARKET.summ: Despite an early start to harvest, steady shipments and cold storage supplies are in position to keep California table grapes available for holiday promotions
takeaways: The California Table Grape Commission says California grapes will stay in promotable volumes through December despite an early harvest.
Harvest is expected to end in mid-November, but shipments will continue well beyond the final picking day.
Commission research found 72% of grape purchasers prefer U.S.-grown grapes, versus fewer than 5% preferring imports.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads Liv-ex trade as Lynch-Bages 2005 becomes top-traded wine
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux led the Liv-ex market with a 37.4% share of purchases, while Burgundy fell to 15.4%.
Lynch-Bages was the region's top-traded wine overall, with the 2005 vintage the most traded across all regions.
US buyers claimed over half of Bordeaux's purchased value, with California-led US share rising from 7.0% to 9.6% overall.

CULTURE.head: Portland's Papi serves Pornstar Martini riff topped with Cava custard foam
CULTURE.summ: It’s no secret that foam is among the most popular drink garnishes of today. From cloud-topped coffees and side-pulled beer pours to frozen cocktails with dollops of salted mascarpone, frothy drinks are popping up in just about every corner of the beverage sector. Bartenders, baristas, and consumers alike just can’t get enough...
takeaways: Izzy Stein, beverage and creative director at Papi in Portland, Maine, created the Mami Chula cocktail.
The cocktail is a rum-based Pornstar Martini riff with passion fruit, lime, and a Cava custard foam topping.
Stein reduces Cava about 40 percent and folds it into an egg yolk, cream, and vanilla custard charged in an iSi canister.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives' wine choices reveal mass-market, sweet-leaning taste
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Cake Zine essay by a certified wine specialist argues Real Housewives favour mass-market, sweet, high-alcohol wines, often Californian cabernet.
Example cited: Whitney Rose recommends Justin Cabernet, a roughly $22 bottle, to a wealthy Salt Lake City castmate.
Author links the taste to Robert Parker's 100-point scoring, which encouraged fruit-forward, lower-acid wines.

SCIENCE.head: Roller-crimped cover crops improve Mediterranean vine water status and mycorrhizal colonization
SCIENCE.summ: In a 2026 study published in Field Crops Research based on Mediterranean rainfed vineyards, the authors found that roller-crimping cover crops improved soil cover, vine water status, yield (in wetter conditions), and mycorrhizal colonization without affecting grape quality, while seasonal climate was the dominant driver of...
takeaways: A 2026 Field Crops Research study tested roller-crimped cover crops in rainfed Mediterranean vineyards.
Roller-crimping improved soil cover, vine water status, and mycorrhizal colonization without affecting grape quality.
Yield rose only in wetter seasons, while seasonal climate was the main driver of fungal diversity.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Traditional labels? Suck my duck
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Never say that wine labelling regulations are a subject devoid of humour. The Tribunal Correctionnel de Paris recently heard a case brought by anti-alcohol NGO Addictions France against Languedoc vigneron Nicolas Vellas over his provocative packaging. Vellas’s edgy cuvées have included “Little Fuck,” “Bad Angel” (its label...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: A Paris court heard a case by anti-alcohol group Addictions France against Languedoc vigneron Nicolas Vellas over his provocative labels, including "Suck my Duck".
Bordeaux has lost a fifth of its vineyard area in four years, with 30,000 ha due to be uprooted by end of December.
Author Tim Atkin argues French wine's conservative labels, especially in Bordeaux, risk alienating younger consumers, while Santus in Franciacorta cites its label for success in Japan.

NEWSLETTERS.head: The 2026 Harvest Is In , Here’s What It’s Already Telling Us About this Burgundy Wine Vintage
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Early harvest data from the 2026 Burgundy vintage reveals exciting insights into the region's grapes, offering a first look at vine yields and pricing
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: Burgundy's Côte d'Or picking finished between 10 and 12 September 2026, after the region's earliest harvest ever recorded.
The Comité des Vins de Bourgogne estimates the 2026 crop down around 30 per cent against the five-year average, with the official figure due mid-November.
Agreste forecasts Pinot Noir losses in Burgundy above half, while Champagne's harvest is seen down by almost half.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Exploring the Roussillon (7) Château Nadal Hainaut
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Château Nadal Hainaut, an organic wine producer in the Roussillon making some nice wines. This visit was with Pauline Nadal,
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Château Nadal Hainaut in the Roussillon farms 27 hectares of vines organically across 10 varieties, including a centenarian Carignan plot.
Pauline Nadal, a sixth-generation family member and trained ceramicist, is responsible for production at the estate.
The estate was bought by the Hainault family in 1826 and rebuilt by Pauline's parents, who still invest in it.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Albarino? Soleri? Pinot Iskra? New White Wine Player in China
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Attendees of the China Sommelier Summit in Shanghai were treated to a new local white wine producer pouring smack dab in the middle of the
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jim Boyce
takeaways: Lan Yue, established in Yantai in 2021, poured six wines at the China Sommelier Summit in Shanghai, including Albarino, Chardonnay, Viognier, Pinot Iskra and Soleri.
Lan Yue planted its first vines in 2023 and recently released its first wines, with its vineyards covering about 15.5 hectares, 2.7 hectares of which are Albarino.
Lan Yue wines are unoaked except the Chardonnay Reserve, and the Albarino is singled out for high acidity and citrus and white flower aromas.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Essential Kit for Kitchen Season
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Outfitting your kitchen with the season’s essential tools, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Meg Maker says the clocks dropping back on Sunday marks the start of what she calls Kitchen Season.
Kitchen Season, she writes, is when November and December cooking becomes a way to mark occasions and cook for others.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Tasting Diaries: October 2026
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Niagara’s Cabernet Franc harvest finally gets underway, plus the bottles that made my October memorable
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Buttonwood Grove's 2025 Blanc de Franc from the Finger Lakes is a white Cabernet Franc the author describes as delicious, with about 10 g/L residual sugar.
Château de Fosse Sèche's 2018 Éolithe VDF from Saumur is praised for freshness and restraint in a warm vintage, with at least five years of life ahead.
Fogolar Wines' 2018 Cabernet Franc Picone Vineyard from Vinemount Ridge, Niagara, is called a serious, cellar-worthy Niagara Cabernet Franc.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A deeper look at underwater wine aging
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Is a wine from the depths ‘better’ or does it depend on the boat?
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Attis, a winery owned by the Fariña family in O Grove, Galicia, ages its Albariño 'Mar' bottles underwater in the estuary.
The Attis Albariño 'Mar' is aged five months underwater at 13-16°C, versus the 'Standard' bottling of about 120,000 annually.
The author's past tastings of underwater-aged wines suggested they seemed older and less fresh than landbound counterparts.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Marion Granges-Faiss and her late husband Jacky farm Domaine de Beudon at 890 metres in Valais, Switzerland, with six hectares of vineyard.
Jacky bought the estate in 1971, and the family became Valais's first Demeter-certified estate in 1992.
Jacky began making his own wine in 1995 with help from Pierre-Antoine Crettenand, since 2003 using only sulphites and bottling unfiltered.
